los.text: Identify and side a tibia, describing the main anatomical landmarks on bones and radiographs
los.html:
Proximal
  • Medial and lateral condyles (plateaus; medial larger and oval)
  • Intercondylar eminence (cruciates and menisci attach in front of and behind it)
  • Tibial tuberosity (patellar ligament)
  • Gerdy's tubercle (iliotibial tract)
  • Fibular facet under the lateral condyle.
ShaftTriangular; anterior border and medial surface are subcutaneous (shin: open fractures common); soleal line behind.
DistalMedial malleolus, fibular notch (inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis), surface for the talus.
SidingMedial malleolus on the inner side; tuberosity at the front; fibular facet behind and lateral.
On X-rayLateral plateau fractures (valgus force); tibial tuberosity irregularity (Osgood–Schlatter in adolescents).

los.text: Identify and side a fibula, describing the main anatomical landmarks and associations with the tibia on bones and radiographs
los.html:
• Head (biceps femoris and lateral collateral ligament attach)
    • neck (the common fibular nerve winds round it)
    • shaft (muscle attachment; carries only ~10–15% of body weight)
    • lateral malleolus (lower than the medial; fibular tendons groove behind it).
Joint with tibiaType
Superior tibiofibularSynovial plane
Interosseous membraneFibrous
Inferior tibiofibularFibrous syndesmosis: holds the ankle mortise
Not part of the knee joint.
SidingThe lateral malleolus's flat articular facet faces medially, with the malleolar fossa behind.
On X-rayWeber ankle fractures by level of the fibular fracture (A below, B at, C above the syndesmosis).

los.text: Identify a patella, locating attachments of quadriceps femoris and ligamentum patellae
los.html:
Largest sesamoid bone, in the quadriceps tendon.
Base(top)Quadriceps tendon attaches. Apex (bottom): patellar ligament begins → tibial tuberosity.
Back
  • Larger lateral facet and medial facet against the femoral trochlea
  • The prominent lateral femoral condyle and vastus medialis obliquus resist lateral dislocation.
FunctionsLengthens the quadriceps lever arm (mechanical advantage); protects the joint.
ClinicalLateral dislocation; fracture from a direct blow; bipartite patella (superolateral) can mimic a fracture on X-ray.

los.text: Describe the movements of the knee joint
los.html:
TypeSynovial modified hinge (two tibiofemoral joints + patellofemoral joint).
MovementsFlexion (~135°), extension to 0°, and a little rotation when flexed.
Locking (screw-home)in the last few degrees of extension the femur medially rotates on the planted tibia.
UnlockingPopliteus laterally rotates the femur to begin flexion.

los.text: Label a diagram of the key ligaments and deep structures of the knee joint
los.html:
StructureAttachmentsRole / test
ACLAnterior tibial intercondylar area → lateral femoral condyle (inner side, back)Stops the tibia sliding forwards; Lachman, anterior drawer
PCLPosterior tibial intercondylar area → medial femoral condyle (inner side, front)Stops the tibia sliding backwards (stronger); posterior sag
MCL (tibial collateral)Medial epicondyle → medial tibia; fused to the medial meniscusResists valgus
LCL (fibular collateral)Lateral epicondyle → fibular head; separate from the lateral meniscus (popliteus tendon between)Resists varus
Medial meniscusC-shaped, bigger, tethered to the MCLLess mobile → torn more often
Lateral meniscusNearly O-shaped, mobile
MenisciDeepen the surfaces, absorb shock, spread load; only the outer "red zone" has a blood supply (heals).
OthersPatellar ligament, oblique popliteal ligament, infrapatellar fat pad, transverse ligament.
Unhappy triadACL + MCL + medial meniscus.

los.text: Identify and describe the actions of the muscles at the knee joint (flexors and extensors) summarising their innervations and main attachments
los.html:
GroupMusclesAttachmentsNerve
ExtensorsQuadriceps femoris: rectus femoris (AIIS; also flexes hip), vastus lateralis, medialis, intermedius→ quadriceps tendon → patella → patellar ligament → tibial tuberosityFemoral (L2–4)
FlexorsHamstrings: biceps femoris (long head ischial tuberosity, short head linea aspera → fibular head), semitendinosus, semimembranosus (ischial tuberosity → medial tibia)Sciatic: tibial part (short head of biceps: common fibular)
Other flexorsGastrocnemius (femoral condyles → calcaneus), sartorius, gracilis, popliteusTibial; femoral; obturator; tibial
Rotation (knee flexed)Medial = semitendinosus, semimembranosus, sartorius, gracilis, popliteus; lateral = biceps femoris.
Pes anserinus(medial tibia)Sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus ("Say Grace before Tea").

los.text: Describe the factors that are responsible for the stability at the knee joint including the locking mechanism close to full extension of the lower limb
los.html:
• Bony stability is poor (flat tibial plateaus), so the knee relies on soft tissues.
StabiliserContribution
Cruciate ligamentsFront-to-back
Collateral ligamentsSide-to-side
MenisciDeepen the surfaces
Capsule and posterior ligamentsResist hyperextension
Quadriceps (especially vastus medialis)The most important muscular stabiliser
Hamstrings, iliotibial tractDynamic support
Locking mechanism
  • in the last ~30° of extension the femur rotates medially on the tibia because the medial condyle's surface is longer
  • The ligaments wind tight and the knee locks, so you can stand with little muscle effort.
UnlockingPopliteus laterally rotates the femur (or medially rotates the tibia when off the ground).

los.text: Explain what structures in close relation to the knee joint (including bursae) may be injured with trauma to the knee (including fractures, dislocation and ruptured cruciate ligaments)
los.html:
InjuryMechanismStructures hurt
ACL rupturePivoting on a planted foot, hyperextension; "pop", swelling within ~2 h (haemarthrosis)± MCL and medial meniscus
PCL tearDashboard: backward blow on the flexed kneePCL
MCL sprainValgus blow to the outer kneeMCL ± medial meniscus
Meniscal tearTwisting on a flexed, loaded kneeLocking, slower swelling, joint line tenderness
Fibular neck fractureDirect blowCommon fibular nerve → foot drop, numb dorsum of foot
Knee dislocationHigh energyPopliteal artery (tethered above and below): check pulses and ABPI; common fibular nerve
Supracondylar femur fractureFall in the elderlyGastrocnemius pulls the fragment back onto the popliteal artery
BursaProblem
Prepatellar"Housemaid's knee" (kneeling)
Superficial infrapatellar"Clergyman's knee"
SuprapatellarCommunicates with the joint: fills with an effusion
Semimembranosus–gastrocnemiusBaker's cyst behind the knee

los.text: Locate the popliteal fossa and identify its boundaries and the structures within it
los.html:
BoundaryFormed by
SuperomedialSemimembranosus and semitendinosus
SuperolateralBiceps femoris
Inferomedial / inferolateralMedial / lateral heads of gastrocnemius
RoofSkin, popliteal fascia (pierced by the small saphenous vein)
FloorPopliteal surface of femur, capsule, popliteus
Contents (superficial → deep)
  • Tibial nerve
  • Common fibular nerve (along the biceps tendon)
  • Popliteal vein
  • Popliteal artery (deepest, on the femur)
  • Small saphenous vein ending
  • Popliteal lymph nodes
  • Fat.
ClinicalFeel the popliteal pulse deep with the knee flexed; popliteal aneurysm (the commonest peripheral aneurysm); Baker's cyst; DVT.

los.text: Discuss the functions and importance of joints
los.html:
Functions of joints
  • Allow movement (range depends on type)
  • Transmit and absorb load
  • Give stability
  • Allow growth (cartilaginous growth plates)
  • Provide proprioception
  • Let the skull mould at birth.
Trade-offMore mobility means less stability (shoulder vs hip).
ImportanceJoint disease (arthritis) is a leading cause of pain and long-term disability.

los.text: Describe the basic structure, biomechanics, nerve and blood supply of synovial joints, and be able to label a diagram of such
los.html:
Structure
  • Hyaline articular cartilage on the bone ends
  • Joint cavity with synovial fluid
  • Fibrous capsule lined by synovial membrane (which doesn't cover the cartilage)
  • Ligaments
  • ± discs/menisci, labra, fat pads, bursae.
BiomechanicsVery low friction (cartilage + fluid: hyaluronan and lubricin); spreads load; stability from bone shape, ligaments and muscles (dynamic).
Blood supplyPeriarticular arterial anastomoses (e.g. the genicular anastomosis) to the capsule and synovium; cartilage is avascular, fed by synovial fluid.
Nerve supply (Hilton's law)
  • The nerves to the muscles moving a joint also supply the joint and its overlying skin
  • Capsule rich in proprioceptors and pain fibres
  • Cartilage has none.
Referred painHip disease can present as knee pain (shared obturator and femoral supply).

los.text: Explain the significance of bursae and ligaments
los.html:
Bursae
  • Closed synovial-lined sacs of fluid that cut friction where tendon, muscle or skin moves over bone (prepatellar, subacromial, olecranon, trochanteric)
  • Some open into the joint (suprapatellar).
BursitisFriction and overuse, infection, gout ("housemaid's knee", "student's elbow").
LigamentsDense regular connective tissue (type I collagen), bone to bone: stabilise and guide movement, limit range, give proprioception.
HealingPoor blood supply → slow; sprains graded I–III; laxity → instability.

los.text: Link the structure of the synovium with its function
los.html:
Intima1–3 cell layers of synoviocytes with no basement membrane: type A (macrophage-like, clear debris), type B (fibroblast-like, make hyaluronan and lubricin).
SubintimaLoose connective tissue rich in fenestrated capillaries and lymphatics.
StructureFunction it gives
Type B cellsSynovial fluid: hyaluronan (viscosity), lubricin (boundary lubrication)
Fenestrated capillaries, no basement membraneFast exchange; nourishes the avascular cartilage; but lets bacteria and inflammatory cells in (septic arthritis, RA pannus)
Type A cellsRemove debris
  • Normal fluid: clear, viscous, few cells (<200/μL); aspiration looks for crystals and infection.

los.text: Describe the processes involved in endochondral ossification and their roles in longitudinal bone growth and fracture healing
los.html:
1. Cartilage modelMesenchyme forms a hyaline cartilage template of the bone.
2. HypertrophyChondrocytes in the shaft enlarge and the matrix calcifies; a periosteal bone collar forms round the shaft.
3. Primary ossification centrea periosteal bud of vessels invades the diaphysis (fetal weeks 7–12); bone is laid on calcified cartilage.
4. Secondary centresin the epiphyses, mostly after birth.
5. Leftover cartilageArticular cartilage and the growth plate between epiphysis and diaphysis.
Growth plate zone (epiphysis → shaft)Event
RestingReserve cells
ProliferativeColumns of dividing chondrocytes: length growth
HypertrophicCells enlarge
CalcificationMatrix calcifies, cells die
OssificationBone laid down
Plate closureAfter puberty (oestrogen) it becomes the epiphyseal line; width grows by periosteal apposition.
Fracture healing repeats it
  • Haematoma → inflammation → soft callus (fibrocartilage) → hard callus (woven bone by endochondral ossification) → remodelling (lamellar bone).
  • Rigid fixation allows direct (primary) healing without callus.
ClinicalSalter–Harris growth plate fractures; achondroplasia (FGFR3, poor proliferation); rickets (failed mineralisation at the plate).
